summary: Specifies a modification to PIM Sparse Mode that lets several routers on a multi-access network share the Designated Router duty instead of one router handling all of it. This spreads the work of tracking listeners and forwarding multicast data.

plainLanguage.summary: One cashier at a shop handles everyone while others stand idle. This lets several cashiers share the line.

subtitle: How several routers on one LAN can share the multicast forwarding work that PIM normally gives to a single Designated Router.

tldr.problem: On a multi-access LAN, one PIM-SM router (the Designated Router) handles all listener tracking and data forwarding. Its links and capacity cap the whole LAN, and if it fails, forwarding for every group has to be rebuilt.
tldr.mechanism: The DR picks a set of Group Designated Router (GDR) candidates and announces them, plus three hash masks, in a new Hello option. A hash over each flow's addresses then picks which candidate builds the forwarding tree for that flow.
tldr.outcome: Different groups can be forwarded by different routers, so bandwidth adds up across routers and a single failure disrupts only a subset of flows. The default modulo hash has poor failover behavior with more than two GDRs.

facts.label: Default masks
facts.value: RP zero; Source and Group all bits set

sections.title: The Single Designated Router Problem
sections.content:
On a multi-access LAN such as Ethernet, PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) elects one router as the Designated Router (DR). For listeners, the DR tracks IGMP or MLD membership reports, starts building source or shared trees, and forwards the data onto the LAN. Because one router does all of this, the LAN's aggregate bandwidth is limited to what that router can handle.

The RFC gives an example with an Ethernet switch and three routers, each with a Gigabit Ethernet link to the switch. If three hosts each ask for 500 Mbps of unique multicast data, that is 1.5 Gbps in total, but a sole DR can push only 1 Gbps through its link, so at least 500 Mbps is lost.

Failover is the second issue. If the only forwarder goes out of service, the newly elected DR has to rebuild forwarding for the whole LAN. If routers forwarded different groups, a failure would disrupt only some flows.
sections.plainLanguage: If one cashier serves the whole shop, the line gets long, and if that cashier goes home, everything stops. Sharing the work between cashiers fixes both problems.

sections.title: GDRs and GDR Candidates
sections.content:
The normal DR election from RFC 7761 is unchanged: the highest DR priority wins, and the IP address breaks ties. On top of that, this RFC adds the Group Designated Router (GDR). For each multicast flow, either (*,G) for Any-Source Multicast or (S,G) for Source-Specific Multicast, a hash picks one router as the GDR, and that router starts building the forwarding tree for the flow.

A GDR Candidate is a router eligible to be picked. To qualify it must advertise the new capability option, use the same hash algorithm as the DR, and have the same DR priority as the DR. In the RFC's example, R4 has a less preferred priority and is left out, and R3 advertises a different hash algorithm and is also left out, leaving R1 and R2 as candidates.

The extension applies only to last-hop routers, those with directly connected receivers. First-hop routers (with directly connected sources) are untouched, because the source tree is built from the sender's address, and an IGP with equal-cost paths already spreads that load.
sections.plainLanguage: Only helpers of the same rank who follow the same rules can join the sharing team. Each toy box (a group) is then given to exactly one helper.

sections.title: Hash Masks and the Modulo Hash
sections.content:
A hash mask chooses which bits of an address feed the hash. There are three: the RP Hash Mask, the Source Hash Mask and the Group Hash Mask. Masks need not be contiguous bits. Implementations SHOULD default the RP mask to zero and the Source and Group masks to all bits set. Masking bits out makes certain flows always land on the same GDR.

The DR lists candidates in the order sent, numbered from 0 to N - 1. The hash result is the ordinal number of the GDR for that flow. The input depends on the flow:

  • ASM group with a nonzero RP mask: hashvalue_RP, based on the RP address.
  • ASM group with a zero RP mask: hashvalue_Group, based on the group address.
  • SSM group: hashvalue_SG, combining source and group.

The modulo hash applies the mask, shifts right by the number of trailing zero bits in the mask, keeps the last 32 bits, and takes the result modulo the number of candidates. For hashvalue_SG, the source and group values are XORed first. A 1-octet Hash Algorithm field allows other algorithms; value 0 is this one.

The RFC states two limits. With more than two GDRs, when one fails, all groups may be reassigned to a different GDR, even those not assigned to the failed one. And at most 32 consecutive bits of the addresses are used, which may matter for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: To decide who gets each toy box, you do a little arithmetic on the box's label and use the answer as the helper's number. The same label always gives the same helper.

sections.title: The Two PIM Hello Options
sections.content:
Two new PIM Hello options carry the information. The DRLB-Cap option (type 34, length 4) says a router supports load balancing and names its hash algorithm. It MUST be sent on all interfaces where DR Load Balancing is enabled, at most once per Hello.

The DRLB-List option (type 35) is sent only by the elected DR. It holds the Group Mask, Source Mask and RP Mask, followed by the GDR Candidate addresses. Its length is (3 + n) x (4 or 16) bytes for n candidates. Masks MUST be the same size as the IP source address of the Hello, and addresses MUST be in the same family. Candidates are recommended to be sorted in descending order so the result is predictable whatever order the DR learned of them.

If a candidate's Hello carries the Interface ID option from RFC 6395 with a nonzero Router Identifier, that identifier forms its candidate address. Otherwise the Hello's source address is used. A DRLB-List received from a non-DR MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: One note says "I can help, and here is how I count." The boss helper sends a second note listing who is on the team and how to count.

sections.title: DR and GDR Candidate Behavior
sections.content:
The DR SHOULD add any neighbor with the same hash algorithm and the same DR priority to its candidate list, and SHOULD include itself, though policy may limit the set. If a listed neighbor expires, stops sending DRLB-Cap, or changes priority or algorithm, the DR SHOULD immediately send a triggered Hello with an updated list. A new eligible candidate is not urgent and appears in the next Hello.

A router acts as a GDR Candidate only if it appears in the DR's list, and it MUST use the DR's masks even if configured differently. When the list or masks change, each candidate re-runs the hash for the groups (or source and group pairs, for SSM) that have local receiver interest. A router that becomes the GDR MUST build the multicast forwarding tree. A router that stops being the GDR uses a modified Assert.

The Assert modification avoids loss during handover. A router that stops being GDR MUST use Assert metric preference 0x7fffffff and metric 0xfffffffe for that group, so the new GDR, with normal metrics, wins the Assert. The old router can keep forwarding while the new one builds its tree, trading a small amount of duplicate traffic for less packet loss.

If the DR does not support the feature, there is no load balancing. Non-DR routers that lack it are simply not candidates.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new helper takes over a box, the old helper keeps working a little while and then steps aside. A little double work is better than dropping anything.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
An administrator should find a set of routers whose combined capacity covers the total bandwidth, with each able to handle its share, and ideally enough left over to survive the failure of at least one router. All routers should reach sources and RPs by paths that are not via the LAN.

Usually the same masks are configured on every router, so the result does not depend on which one becomes DR. The RP Hash Mask must be set if hashing should follow the RP address rather than the group address for ASM. Only routers announcing the same hash algorithm as the DR are candidates, and migration between algorithms is not covered by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure the whole team together can carry everything, even if one helper is out sick.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new options are only as secure as PIM Hello messages, so the considerations in RFC 7761 apply. A subverted DR could omit or add GDRs or announce an unsupported algorithm. A subverted router could be made DR and cause the same issues. The RFC notes this is not very different from existing attacks, such as subverting a DR and lowering its priority.

If the DR lists a candidate that announces a different algorithm, that candidate ignores the list, and no router handles the flows that hash to it. An attacker could also send one high-rate flow, or many flows expected to hash to the same GDR.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad actor becomes the boss helper, they can give out the wrong jobs, so the team has to trust its boss.
